prompt: A city predicts commute time from distance, departure time, and weather. Describe the statistical-learning relationship using X, f, and an error term, and explain why two identical X values might still have different outcomes.
A company asks whether discounts cause higher sales, while another team only wants next week's best sales forecast. Identify the primary objective in each case and discuss one modeling consequence.
Suppose a predictor uses every relevant recorded feature but outcomes still vary. Explain why irreducible error may remain and how you would recognize improvement in the reducible part.

You have a small noisy dataset and must choose between a simple assumed functional form and a highly flexible local method. Compare the risks and justify what additional evidence would guide your choice.
As model complexity rises, training error keeps falling while validation error first falls and then rises. Explain the pattern and how you would choose a model if interpretation is also important.
A researcher groups documents by word patterns without labels and later predicts a known topic label. Explain which stage is unsupervised and which is supervised.
An algorithm outputs both the probability of disease and a yes-or-no diagnosis. Explain why the underlying target makes this primarily a classification task even though one output is numeric.
Model A has training MSE 2 and test MSE 12; Model B has training MSE 5 and test MSE 7. Which better generalizes, and what can and cannot be concluded from these four numbers?
A fitted curve changes dramatically when a few training cases are replaced. Relate this behavior to variance, bias, and expected test error, then name one possible response.
A KNN model uses a very small K in a region with noisy labels. Predict how increasing K could change its decision boundary and test behavior, including one possible downside.
For fitted equation y-hat = 10 + 2x, interpret both coefficients in context, define the residual for one case, and explain why the residual is not the same as the population error term.
A slope estimate is 1.2 with a 95% confidence interval from -0.1 to 2.5. Explain what this suggests about the usual zero-slope test and why it does not prove no relationship exists.
Two response variables use different units, and their regressions have residual standard errors 3 and 20. Explain why the raw numbers alone do not tell which model fits better.
A model reports R-squared 0.95 but performs poorly on new data. Give plausible reasons and explain why R-squared alone is not a generalization metric.
A predictor has a positive slope alone but a negative coefficient after another correlated predictor is added. Explain how this can happen without saying that one estimate must be a software error.
You need uncertainty for the average demand of similar stores and for demand at one new store. State which interval answers each question and why their widths differ.
A regression uses three region indicators incorrectly together with an intercept. Explain the redundancy, how to choose a reference region, and how changing the reference affects fitted values.
A treatment effect becomes larger as baseline risk increases. Explain how an interaction term can represent this and contrast it with an additive model.
Residuals fan out as fitted values increase but show no curve. Identify the main issue, distinguish it from non-linearity, and state what part of linear-model reasoning it threatens.

Case A has an unusual predictor value but lies near the fitted line; Case B has ordinary predictors but a very large residual. Classify their leverage and outlier status and discuss possible influence.

A regression gives large standard errors for two related predictors, but their joint F-test is strong. Explain how collinearity can produce this pattern and what not to conclude about their joint predictive value.
